If it was such a comfort to him as he had lately intimated, that they had hitherto <hi type="italic">continued with him</hi> in his lesser trials (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.28">Luke xxii. 28</reference>), we may well imagine what a grief it was to him, that they deserted him now in the greatest, when they might have done him some service—when he was abused, to protect him, and when accused, to witness for him. Let not those that suffer for Christ, think it strange, if they be thus deserted, and if all the herd shun the wounded deer; they are not better than their Master, nor can expect to be better used either by their enemies or by their friends. When St. Paul was in peril, none <hi type="italic">stood by him,</hi> but <hi type="italic">all men forsook him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2 Tim. iv. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen24978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24979" type="x-p"/> IX. The noise disturbed the neighbourhood, and some of the neighbours were brought into danger by the riot, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.51-Mark.14.52">v. 51, 52</reference>. This passage of story we have not in any other of the evangelists. Here is an account of a <hi type="italic">certain young man,</hi> who, as it should seem, was no disciple of Christ, nor, as some have imagined, a servant of the house wherein Christ had eaten the passover, who <hi type="italic">followed him</hi> to see what would become of him (as the <hi type="italic">sons of the prophets,</hi> when they understood that Elijah was to be <hi type="italic">taken up,</hi> went to <hi type="italic">view afar off,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.7">2 Kings ii. 7</reference>), but some young man that lived near the garden, perhaps in the house to which the garden belonged. Now observe concerning him, <div eID="gen24979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24980" type="x-p"/> 1. How he was <hi type="italic">frightened out of his bed,</hi> to be a <hi type="italic">spectator</hi> of Christ's sufferings. Such a <hi type="italic">multitude,</hi> so armed, and coming with so much fury, and in the dead of night, and in a quiet village, could not but produce a great stir; this alarmed our <hi type="italic">young man,</hi> who perhaps thought they was some tumult or rising in the city, some <hi type="italic">uproar among the people,</hi> and had the curiosity to go, and see what the matter was, and was in such haste to inform himself, that he could not stay to dress himself, but threw a sheet about him, as if he would appear like a walking ghost, in grave clothes, to frighten those who had frightened him, and ran among the thickest of them with this question, <hi type="italic">What is to do here?</hi> Being told, he had a mind to see the issue, having, no doubt, heard much of the fame of this Jesus; and therefore, when all his disciples had quitted him, he continued to <hi type="italic">follow him,</hi> desirous to <hi type="italic">hear</hi> what he would say, and <hi type="italic">see</hi> what he would do. Some think that his having no other garment than this <hi type="italic">linen cloth</hi> upon his naked body, intimates that he was one of those Jews who made a great profession of piety that their neighbours, in token of which, among other instances of austerity and mortification of the body, they used no clothes but one linen garment, which, though contrived to be modest enough, was thin and cold. But I rather think that this was not his constant wear. <div eID="gen24980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24981" type="x-p"/> 2. See how he was <hi type="italic">frightened into his bed</hi> again, when he was in danger of being made a <hi type="italic">sharer</hi> in Christ's sufferings. His own disciples had run away from him; but this young man, having no concern for him, thought he might securely attend him, especially being so far from being armed, that he was not so much as clothed; but <hi type="italic">the young men,</hi> the Roman soldiers, who were called to assist, <hi type="italic">laid hold of him,</hi> for all was fish that came to their net. Perhaps they were now vexed at themselves, that they had suffered the disciples to <hi type="italic">run away,</hi> and they being got out of their reach they resolved to seize the first they could <hi type="italic">lay their hands on;</hi> though this young man was perhaps one of the <hi type="italic">strictest sect</hi> of the Jewish church, yet the Roman soldiers made no conscience of abusing him upon this occasion. Finding himself in danger, he <hi type="italic">left the linen cloth</hi> by which they had <hi type="italic">caught hold of him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">fled away naked.</hi> This passage is recorded to show what a barbarous crew this was, that was sent to seize Christ, and what a narrow escape the disciples had of falling into their hands, out of which nothing could have kept them but their Master's care of them; <hi type="italic">If ye seek me, let these go their way,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.8">John xviii. 8</reference>. It also intimates that there is <hi type="italic">no hold</hi> of those who are led by curiosity only, and not by faith and conscience, to follow Christ.
entries.07cd3d20a5e3f2152984ad7700e9f32ede60359d: <div eID="gen24981" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Brought before the High Priest.</title> <div sID="gen24982" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">53</hi> And they led Jesus away to the high priest: and with him were assembled all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes. <hi type="super">54</hi> And Peter followed him afar off, even into the palace of the high priest: and he sat with the servants, and warmed himself at the fire. <hi type="super">55</hi> And the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none. <hi type="super">56</hi> For many bare false witness against him, but their witness agreed not together. <hi type="super">57</hi> And there arose certain, and bare false witness against him, saying, 58 We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and within three days I will build another made without hands. <hi type="super">59</hi> But neither so did their witness agree together. 60 And the high priest stood up in the midst, and asked Jesus, saying, Answerest thou nothing? what <hi type="italic">is it which</hi> these witness against thee? <hi type="super">61</hi> But he held his peace, and answered nothing. Again the high priest asked him, and said unto him, Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? <hi type="super">62</hi> And Jesus said, I am: and ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven. <hi type="super">63</hi> Then the high priest rent his clothes, and saith, What need we any further witnesses? <hi type="super">64</hi> Ye have heard the blasphemy: what think ye? And they all condemned him to be guilty of death. <hi type="super">65</hi> And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to buffet him, and to say unto him, Prophesy: and the servants did strike him with the palms of their hands. <div eID="gen24982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24983" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's arraignment, trial, conviction, and condemnation, in the <hi type="italic">ecclesiastical</hi> court, before the great sanhedrim, of which the <hi type="italic">high priest</hi> was president, or judge of the court; the same Caiaphas that had lately adjudged it expedient he should be put to death, guilty or not guilty (<reference osisRef="John.11.50">John xi. 50</reference>), and who therefore might justly be excepted against as partial. <div eID="gen24983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24984" type="x-p"/> I. Christ is hurried away to his <hi type="italic">house,</hi> his <hi type="italic">palace</hi> it is called, such state did he live in. And there, though, in the dead of the night, <hi type="italic">all the chief priests, and elders, and scribes,</hi> that were in the secret, were <hi type="italic">assembled,</hi> ready to receive the prey; so sure were they of it. <div eID="gen24984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24985" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">Peter followed</hi> at a distance, such a degree of cowardice was his late courage dwindled into, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.54">v. 54</reference>. But when he came to the high priest's palace, he <hi type="italic">sneakingly</hi> went, and <hi type="italic">sat with the servants,</hi> that he might not be suspected to belong to Christ. The high priest's fire side was no proper place, nor his servants proper company, for Peter, but it was his <hi type="italic">entrance into a temptation.</hi> <div eID="gen24985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24986" type="x-p"/> III. Great diligence was used to procure, for love or money, false witnesses against Christ. They had seized him as a malefactor, and now they had him they had no indictment to prefer against him, no crime to lay to his charge, but they <hi type="italic">sought for witnesses against him;</hi> pumped some with ensnaring questions, offered bribes to others, if they <hi type="italic">would accuse him,</hi> and endeavored to frighten others, if they <hi type="italic">would not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.55-Mark.14.56">v. 55, 56</reference>. The chief priests and elders were by the law entrusted with the prosecuting and punishing of <hi type="italic">false witnesses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.19.16-Deut.19.17">Deut. xix. 16, 17</reference>); yet those were now ringleaders in a crime that tends to overthrow of all justice. It is time to cry, <hi type="italic">Help, Lord,</hi> when the physicians of a land are its troublers, and those that should be the conservators of peace and equity, are the corrupters of both. <div eID="gen24986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24987" type="x-p"/> IV. He was at length charged with words spoken some years ago, which, as they were represented, seemed to threaten <hi type="italic">the temple,</hi> which they had made no better than an idol of (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.57-Mark.14.58">v. 57, 58</reference>); but the witnesses to this matter did not agree (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.59">v. 59</reference>), for one swore that he said, <hi type="italic">I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days</hi> (so it is in Matthew); the other swore that he said, <hi type="italic">I will destroy this temple, that is made with hands,</hi> and <hi type="italic">within three days, I will build</hi> not it, but <hi type="italic">another made without hands;</hi> now these two differ much from each other; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oude ise en he martyria</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">their testimony was not sufficient,</hi> nor equal to the charge of a capital crime; so Dr. Hammond: they did not accuse him of that upon which a <hi type="italic">sentence of death</hi> might be founded, no not by the utmost stretch of their law. <div eID="gen24987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24988" type="x-p"/> V. He was urged to be his own accuser (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.60">v. 60</reference>); The <hi type="italic">high priest stood up</hi> in a heat, and said, <hi type="italic">Answerest thou nothing?</hi> This he said under pretence of justice and fair dealing, but really with a design to ensnare him, that they might <hi type="italic">accuse him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.53-Luke.11.54">Luke xi. 53, 54</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.20">xx. 20</reference>. We may well imagine with what an air of haughtiness and disdain this proud high priest brought our Lord Jesus to this question; "Come you, the prisoner at the bar, you hear what is sworn against you; what have you now to say for yourself?" Pleased to think that <hi type="italic">he</hi> seemed silent, who had so often silenced those that picked quarrels with him. Still Christ <hi type="italic">answered nothing,</hi> that he might set us an example, 1. Of <hi type="italic">patience</hi> under calumnies and false accusations; when we are <hi type="italic">reviled,</hi> let us not <hi type="italic">revile again,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.23">1 Pet. ii. 23</reference>. And, 2. Of <hi type="italic">prudence,</hi> when a man shall be made an <hi type="italic">offender for a word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa. xxix. 21</reference>), and our <hi type="italic">de</hi>fence made our <hi type="italic">of</hi>fence; it is an evil time indeed when the prudent shall <hi type="italic">keep silence</hi> (lest they make bad worse), <hi type="italic">and commit their cause to him that judgeth righteously.</hi> But, <div eID="gen24988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24989" type="x-p"/> VI. When he was asked <hi type="italic">whether he was the Christ,</hi> he confessed, and denied not, that <hi type="italic">he was,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.61-Mark.14.62">v. 61, 62</reference>. He asked, <hi type="italic">Art thou the Son of the Blessed?</hi> that is the Son of <hi type="italic">God?</hi> for, as Dr. Hammond observes, the Jews, when they named <hi type="italic">God,</hi> generally added, <hi type="italic">blessed for ever;</hi> and thence <hi type="italic">the Blessed</hi> is the title of <hi type="italic">God,</hi> a peculiar title, and applied to Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Rom. ix. 5</reference>. And for the proof of his being the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> he binds them over to his second coming; "<hi type="italic">Ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power;</hi> that <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> that now appears so mean and despicable, whom ye <hi type="italic">see</hi> and trample upon (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2-Isa.53.3">Isa. liii. 2, 3</reference>), you shall shortly see and <hi type="italic">tremble before.</hi>" Now, one would think that such a word as this which our Lord Jesus seems to have spoken with a grandeur and majesty not agreeable to his present appearance (for through the thickest cloud of his humiliation some rays of glory were still darted forth), should have startled the court, and at least, in the opinion of some of them, should have amounted to a <hi type="italic">demurrer,</hi> or <hi type="italic">arrest of judgment,</hi> and that they should have stayed process till they had considered further of it; when Paul at the bar reasoned of the <hi type="italic">judgment to come,</hi> the judge <hi type="italic">trembled,</hi> and adjourned the trial, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.25">Acts xxiv. 25</reference>. But these chief priests were so miserably blinded with malice and rage, that, like the horse rushing into the battle, they <hi type="italic">mocked at fear, and were not affrighted,</hi> neither <hi type="italic">believed they that it was the sound of the trumpet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.22">Job xxxix. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">24</reference>. And see <reference osisRef="Job.15.25-Job.15.26">Job xv. 25, 26</reference>. <div eID="gen24989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24990" type="x-p"/> VII. The high priest, upon this confession of his, convicted him as a <hi type="italic">blasphemer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.63">v. 63</reference>); He <hi type="italic">rent his clothes</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">chitonas autou</hi></hi>. Some think the word signifies his pontifical vestments, which, for the greater state, he had put on, though in the night, upon this occasion. As before, in his enmity to Christ, he said he knew not what (<reference osisRef="John.11.51-John.11.52">John xi. 51, 52</reference>), so now he did he knew not what. If Saul's rending Samuel's mantle was made to signify the rending of the kingdom from him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.27-1Sam.15.28">1 Sam. xv. 27, 28</reference>), much more did Caiaphas's rending his own clothes signify the rending of the priesthood from him, as the rending of the veil, at Christ's death, signified the throwing of all open. Christ's clothes, even when he was crucified, were kept entire, and not rent: for when the Levitical priesthood was rent in pieces and done away, <hi type="italic">This Man, because he continues ever, has an unchangeable priesthood.</hi> <div eID="gen24990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24991" type="x-p"/> VIII. They agreed that he was a blasphemer, and, as such, was guilty of a capital crime, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.64">v. 64</reference>. The question <hi type="italic">seemed</hi> to be put fairly, <hi type="italic">What think ye?</hi> But it was really <hi type="italic">prejudged,</hi> for the high priest had said, <hi type="italic">Ye have heard the blasphemy;</hi> he gave judgment first, who, as president of the court, ought to have voted last. So they <hi type="italic">all condemned him</hi> to be <hi type="italic">guilty of death;</hi> what friends he had in the great sanhedrim, did not appear, it is probable that they had not notice. <div eID="gen24991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24992" type="x-p"/> IX. They set themselves to abuse him, and, as the Philistines with Samson, to make sport with him, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.65">v. 65</reference>. It should seem that some of the priests themselves that had condemned him, so far forgot the dignity, as well as duty, of their place, and the gravity which became them, that they helped their servants in playing the fool with a condemned prisoner. This they made their diversion, while they <hi type="italic">waited for the morning,</hi> to complete their villany. That <hi type="italic">night of observations</hi> (as the passover-night was called) they <hi type="italic">made a merry night of.</hi> If they did not think it below them to abuse Christ, shall we think any thing below us, by which we may do him honour?
entries.2ecdb1ee060a683b5dff6a744d3b3acb980c88ee: <div eID="gen24992" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Fall.</title> <div sID="gen24993" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">66</hi> And as Peter was beneath in the palace, there cometh one of the maids of the high priest: <hi type="super">67</hi> And when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked upon him, and said, And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth. <hi type="super">68</hi> But he denied, saying, I know not, neither understand I what thou sayest. And he went out into the porch; and the cock crew. <hi type="super">69</hi> And a maid saw him again, and began to say to them that stood by, This is <hi type="italic">one</hi> of them. <hi type="super">70</hi> And he denied it again. And a little after, they that stood by said again to Peter, Surely thou art <hi type="italic">one</hi> of them: for thou art a Galilæan, and thy speech agreeth <hi type="italic">thereto.</hi> <hi type="super">71</hi> But he began to curse and to swear, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> I know not this man of whom ye speak. <hi type="super">72</hi> And the second time the cock crew. And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus said unto him, Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. And when he thought thereon, he wept. <div eID="gen24993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24994" type="x-p"/> We have here the story of Peter's denying Christ. <div eID="gen24994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24995" type="x-p"/> 1. It began in <hi type="italic">keeping at a distance</hi> from him. Peter had followed <hi type="italic">afar off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.54">v. 54</reference>), and now was <hi type="italic">beneath in the palace,</hi> at the lower end of the hall. Those that are <hi type="italic">shy</hi> of Christ, are in a fair way to <hi type="italic">deny</hi> him, that are shy of attending on holy ordinances, shy of the communion of the faithful, and loth to be seen on the side of despised godliness. <div eID="gen24995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24996" type="x-p"/> 2. It was occasioned by his associating with the high priest's servants, and sitting among them. They that think it dangerous to be in company with Christ's disciples, because thence they may be drawn in to <hi type="italic">suffer for him,</hi> will find it much more dangerous to be in company with his enemies, because there they may be drawn in to <hi type="italic">sin against him.</hi> <div eID="gen24996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24997" type="x-p"/> 3. The temptation was, his being charged as a disciple of Christ; <hi type="italic">Thou also wert with Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.67">v. 67</reference>. <hi type="italic">This is one of them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.69">v. 69</reference>), <hi type="italic">for thou art a Galilean,</hi> one may know that by thy speaking broad, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.70">v. 70</reference>. It doth not appear that he was <hi type="italic">challenged</hi> upon it, or in danger of being <hi type="italic">prosecuted</hi> as a criminal for it, but only <hi type="italic">bantered</hi> upon it, and in danger of being ridiculed as a fool for it. While the chief priests were abusing the Master, the servants were abusing the disciples. Sometimes the cause of Christ seems to fall so much on the losing side, that every body has a stone to throw at it, and even the <hi type="italic">abjects gather themselves together against</hi> it. When Job was on the dunghill, he was had in derision of those that were the <hi type="italic">children of base men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.8">Job xxx. 8</reference>. Yet, all things considered, the temptation could not be called <hi type="italic">formidable;</hi> it was only a <hi type="italic">maid</hi> that casually cast her eye upon him, and, for aught that appears, without design of giving him any trouble, said, <hi type="italic">Thou art one of them,</hi> to which he needed not to have made any reply, or might have said, "And if I be, I hope that is no treason." <div eID="gen24997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24998" type="x-p"/> 4. The sin was very great; he <hi type="italic">denied Christ before men,</hi> at a time when he ought to have confessed and owned him, and to have appeared in court a witness for him. Christ had often given notice to his disciples of his own sufferings; yet, when they came, they were to Peter as great a surprise and terror as if he had never heard of them before. He had often told them that they must <hi type="italic">suffer</hi> for him, must <hi type="italic">take up their cross,</hi> and follow him; and yet Peter is so terribly afraid of suffering, upon the very first alarm of it, that he will lie and swear, and do any thing, to avoid it. When Christ was admired and flocked after, he could readily own him; but now that he is deserted, and despised, and run down, he is ashamed of him, and will own no relation to him. <div eID="gen24998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24999" type="x-p"/> 5. His repentance was very speedy. He repeated his denial thrice, and the third was worst of all, for then he <hi type="italic">cursed</hi> and <hi type="italic">swore,</hi> to confirm his denial; and that the third blow, which, one would think, should have <hi type="italic">stunned him,</hi> and knocked him down, <hi type="italic">startled him,</hi> and roused him up. Then the <hi type="italic">cock crew</hi> the second time, which put him in mind of his Master's words, the warning he had given him, with that particular circumstance of the <hi type="italic">cock crowing twice;</hi> by recollecting that, he was made sensible of his sin and the aggravations of it; and when he thought thereon, he wept. Some observe that this evangelist, who wrote, as some have thought, by St. Peter's direction, speaks as fully of Peter's sin as any of them, but more briefly of his <hi type="italic">sorrow,</hi> which Peter, in modesty, would not have to be magnified, and because he thought he could never sorrow enough for great a sin. His repentance here is thus expressed, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epibalon eklaie</hi></hi>, where something must be supplied. He <hi type="italic">added to weep,</hi> so some; making it a Hebraism; he wept, and the more he thought of it, the more he wept; he continued weeping; he <hi type="italic">flung out,</hi> and wept; <hi type="italic">burst out</hi> into tears; <hi type="italic">threw himself down,</hi> and wept; he <hi type="italic">covered his face,</hi> and wept, so some; cast his garment about his head, that he might not be seen to weep; he <hi type="italic">cast his eyes</hi> upon his Master, who turned, and looked upon him; so Dr. Hammond supplies it, and it is a probable conjecture. Or, as we understand it, <hi type="italic">fixing his mind upon it,</hi> he wept. It is not a transient thought of that which is humbling, that will suffice, but we must dwell upon it. Or, what if this word should mean his <hi type="italic">laying a load</hi> upon himself, throwing a confusion into his own face? he did as the <hi type="italic">publican</hi> that smote his breast, in sorrow for sin; and this amounts to his weeping bitterly.  <chapter eID="Mark.14"/> <div eID="gen24999" type="x-p"/>

entries.60107527be11ca4000a1c78dcecbd108db79fbf4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14160"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.14.1-Mark.14.11">Mr 14:1-11</reference>. The Conspiracy of the Jewish Authorities to Put Jesus to Death--The Supper and the Anointing at Bethany--Judas Agrees with the Chief Priests to Betray His Lord. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.26.1-Matt.26.16">Mt 26:1-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.1-Luke.22.6">Lu 22:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.1-John.12.11">Joh 12:1-11</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27360" type="x-p"/> The events of this section appeared to have occurred on the fourth day (Wednesday) of the Redeemer's Last Week.<div eID="gen27360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27361" type="x-p"/> Conspiracy of the Jewish Authorities to Put Jesus to Death (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.1">Mr 14:1</reference>, 2).<div eID="gen27361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14160"/><hi type="bold">1. After two days was the feast of the passover, and of unleavened bread--</hi>The meaning is, that two days after what is about to be mentioned the passover would arrive; in other words, what follows occurred two days before the feast.<div eID="gen27362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might take him by craft, and put him to death--</hi>From Matthew's fuller account (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.1-Matt.26.75">Mt 26:1-75</reference>) we learn that our Lord announced this to the Twelve as follows, being the first announcement to them of the precise time: "And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.1">Mt 26:1</reference>)--referring to the contents of <reference osisRef="Matt.24.1-Matt.25.46">Mt 24:1-25:46</reference>, which He delivered to His disciples; His public ministry being now closed: from His prophetical He is now passing into His priestly office, although all along He Himself took our infirmities and bare our sicknesses--"He said unto His disciples, Ye know that after two days is [the feast of] the passover, and the Son of man is betrayed to be crucified." The first and the last steps of His final sufferings are brought together in this brief announcement of all that was to take place. The passover was the first and the chief of the three great annual festivals, commemorative of the redemption of God's people from Egypt, through the sprinkling of the blood of a lamb divinely appointed to be slain for that end; the destroying angel, "when he saw the blood, passing over" the Israelitish houses, on which that blood was seen, when he came to destroy all the first-born in the land of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Ex 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.13">13</reference>)--bright typical foreshadowing of the great Sacrifice, and the Redemption effected thereby. Accordingly, "by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in working," it was so ordered that precisely at the passover season, "Christ our Passover should be sacrificed for us." On the day following the passover commenced "the feast of unleavened bread," so called because for seven days only unleavened bread was to be eaten (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.18-Exod.12.20">Ex 12:18-20</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6-1Cor.5.8">1Co 5:6-8</reference>. We are further told by Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.3">Mt 26:3</reference>) that the consultation was held in the palace of Caiaphas the high priest, between the chief priests, [the scribes], and the elders of the people, how "they might take Jesus by subtlety and kill Him." <div eID="gen27363" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2a822454a0ce12161cf92c9c9ac572e0a0d2c1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14161"/><div sID="gen27364" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14161"/><hi type="bold">2. But they said, Not on the feast day--</hi>rather, not during the feast; not until the seven days of unleavened bread should be over.<div eID="gen27364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest there be an uproar of the people--</hi>In consequence of the vast influx of strangers, embracing all the male population of the land who had reached a certain age, there were within the walls of Jerusalem at this festival some two million people; and in their excited state, the danger of tumult and bloodshed among "the people," who for the most part took Jesus for a prophet, was extreme. See Josephus [Antiquities, 20.5.3]. What plan, if any, these ecclesiastics fixed upon for seizing our Lord, does not appear. But the proposal of Judas being at once and eagerly gone into, it is probable they were till then at some loss for a plan sufficiently quiet and yet effectual. So, just at the feast time shall it be done; the unexpected offer of Judas relieving them of their fears. Thus, as Bengel remarks, did the divine counsel take effect.<div eID="gen27365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> The Supper and the Anointing at Bethany Six Days before the Passover (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.3-Mark.14.9">Mr 14:3-9</reference>).<div eID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27367" type="x-p"/> The time of this part of the narrative is four days before what has just been related. Had it been part of the regular train of events which our Evangelist designed to record, he would probably have inserted it in its proper place, before the conspiracy of the Jewish authorities. But having come to the treason of Judas, he seems to have gone back upon this scene as what probably gave immediate occasion to the awful deed. <div eID="gen27367" type="x-p"/>
entries.13295abd9e1583bd6ee84027d16e6a14cc84fa05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14162"/><div sID="gen27368" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14162"/><hi type="bold">3. And being in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman--</hi>It was "Mary," as we learn from <reference osisRef="John.12.3">Joh 12:3</reference>.<div eID="gen27368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard--</hi>pure nard, a celebrated aromatic--(See <reference osisRef="Song.1.12">So 1:12</reference>).<div eID="gen27369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">very precious--</hi>"very costly" (<reference osisRef="John.12.3">Joh 12:3</reference>).<div eID="gen27370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and she brake the box, and poured it on his head--</hi>"and anointed," adds John (<reference osisRef="John.12.3">Joh 12:3</reference>), "the feet of Jesus, and wiped His feet with her hair: <hi type="bold">and the house was filled with the odor of the ointment." The only use of this was to refresh and exhilarate--</hi>a grateful compliment in the East, amid the closeness of a heated atmosphere, with many guests at a feast. Such was the form in which Mary's love to Christ, at so much cost to herself, poured itself out. <div eID="gen27371" type="x-p"/>
entries.9567ab92ad406fe6b7816b43ef7ae83abfa55e86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14163"/><div sID="gen27372" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14163"/><hi type="bold">4. And there were some that had indignation within themselves and said--</hi>Matthew says (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.8">Mt 26:8</reference>), "But when His disciples saw it, they had indignation, saying," &c. The spokesman, however, was none of the true-hearted Eleven--as we learn from John (<reference osisRef="John.12.4">Joh 12:4</reference>): "Then saith one of His disciples, Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, which should betray Him." Doubtless the thought stirred first in his breast, and issued from his base lips; and some of the rest, ignorant of his true character and feelings, and carried away by his plausible speech, might for the moment feel some chagrin at the apparent waste.<div eID="gen27372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27373" type="x-p"/> Why was this waste of the ointment made? <div eID="gen27373" type="x-p"/>
entries.b19cd3e0cc981f79f57a1366103d3c276e376612: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14164"/><div sID="gen27374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14164"/><hi type="bold">5. For it might have been sold for more than three hundred pence--</hi>between nine and ten pounds sterling.<div eID="gen27374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and have been given to the poor. And they murmured against her--</hi>"This he said," remarks John (<reference osisRef="John.12.6">Joh 12:6</reference>), and the remark is of exceeding importance, "not that he cared for the poor but because he was a thief, and had the bag"--the scrip or treasure chest--"and bare what was put therein"--not "bare it off" by theft, as some understand it. It is true that he did this; but the expression means simply that he had charge of it and its contents, or was treasurer to Jesus and the Twelve. What a remarkable arrangement was this, by which an avaricious and dishonest person was not only taken into the number of the Twelve, but entrusted with the custody of their little property! The purposes which this served are obvious enough; but it is further noticeable, that the remotest hint was never given to the Eleven of his true character, nor did the disciples most favored with the intimacy of Jesus ever suspect him, till a few minutes before he voluntarily separated himself from their company--for ever! <div eID="gen27375" type="x-p"/>
entries.56e898e6d753db49d21cde4152ecafd995cdcae9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14165"/><div sID="gen27376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14165"/><hi type="bold">6. And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me--</hi>It was good in itself, and so was acceptable to Christ; it was eminently seasonable, and so more acceptable still; and it was "what she could," and so most acceptable of all. <div eID="gen27376" type="x-p"/>
entries.b89fdda6abb678e89ca6234fecbcfbf0846fd7da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14166"/><div sID="gen27377" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14166"/><hi type="bold">7. For ye have the poor with you always--</hi>referring to <reference osisRef="Deut.15.11">De 15:11</reference>.<div eID="gen27377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and whensoever ye will ye may do them good: but me ye have not always--</hi>a gentle hint of His approaching departure, by One who knew the worth of His own presence. <div eID="gen27378" type="x-p"/>
entries.0478b09aac24a6796cdf580e2158ab81498e90db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14167"/><div sID="gen27379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14167"/><hi type="bold">8. She hath done what she could--</hi>a noble testimony, embodying a principle of immense importance.<div eID="gen27379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying--</hi>or, as in John (<reference osisRef="John.12.7">Joh 12:7</reference>), "Against the day of my burying hath she kept this." Not that she, dear heart, thought of His burial, much less reserved any of her nard to anoint her dead Lord. But as the time was so near at hand when that office would have to be performed, and she was not to have that privilege even after the spices were brought for the purpose (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.1">Mr 16:1</reference>), He lovingly regards it as done now. "In the act of love done to Him," says Olshausen beautifully, "she has erected to herself an eternal monument, as lasting as the Gospel, the eternal Word of God. From generation to generation this remarkable prophecy of the Lord has been fulfilled; and even we, in explaining this saying of the Redeemer, of necessity contribute to its accomplishment." "Who but Himself," asks Stier, "had the power to ensure to any work of man, even if resounding in His own time through the whole earth, an imperishable remembrance in the stream of history? Behold once more here the majesty of His royal judicial supremacy in the government of the world, in this, 'Verily I say unto you.'" <div eID="gen27380" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1d6af56026f0d130aad63172d557ee4b0786bdc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14168"/><div sID="gen27381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14168"/><hi type="bold">10. And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went unto the chief priests, to betray him unto them--</hi>that is, to make his proposals, and to bargain with them, as appears from Matthew's fuller statement (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.14">Mt 26:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.15">15</reference>) which says, he "went unto the chief priests, and said, What will ye give me, and I will deliver Him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver." The thirty pieces of silver were thirty shekels, the fine paid for man- or maid-servant accidentally killed (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.32">Ex 21:32</reference>), and equal to between four and five pounds sterling--"a goodly price that I was prized at of them!" (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">Zec 11:13</reference>). <div eID="gen27381" type="x-p"/>

And when they heard it, they were glad, and promised to give him money--</hi>Matthew alone records the precise sum, because a remarkable and complicated prophecy, which he was afterwards to refer to, was fulfilled by it.<div eID="gen27382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And he sought how he might conveniently betray him--</hi>or, as more fully given in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.6">Lu 22:6</reference>), "And he promised, and sought opportunity to betray Him unto them in the absence of the multitude." That he should avoid an "uproar" or "riot" among the people, which probably was made an essential condition by the Jewish authorities, was thus assented to by the traitor; into whom, says Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.3">Lu 22:3</reference>), "Satan entered," to put him upon this hellish deed.<div eID="gen27383" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.14.12-Mark.14.26">Mr 14:12-26</reference>. Preparation for, and Last Celebration of, the Passover--Announcement of the Traitor--Institution of the Supper.
