( = <reference osisRef="Matt.26.47-Matt.26.56">Mt 26:47-56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.47-Luke.22.53">Lu 22:47-53</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.18.1-John.18.12">Joh 18:1-12</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27388" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="John.18.1-John.18.12">Joh 18:1-12</reference>.<div eID="gen27388" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.14.53-Mark.14.72">Mr 14:53-72</reference>. Jesus Arraigned before the Sanhedrim, Condemned to Die, and Shamefully Entreated--The Fall of Peter. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.26.57-Matt.26.75">Mt 26:57-75</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.54-Luke.22.71">Lu 22:54-71</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.18.13-John.18.24">Joh 18:13-18, 24</reference>-<reference osisRef="John.18.27">27</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Had we only the first three Gospels, we should have concluded that our Lord was led immediately to Caiaphas, and had before the Council. But as the Sanhedrim could hardly have been brought together at the dead hour of night--</hi>by which time our Lord was in the hands of the officers sent to take Him--and as it was only "as soon as it was day" that the Council met (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.66">Lu 22:66</reference>), we should have had some difficulty in knowing what was done with Him during those intervening hours. In the Fourth Gospel, however, all this is cleared up, and a very important addition to our information is made (<reference osisRef="John.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.19-John.14.24">14, 19-24</reference>). Let us endeavor to trace the events in the true order of succession, and in the detail supplied by a comparison of all the four streams of text.<div eID="gen27389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27390" type="x-p"/> Jesus Is Brought Privately before Annas, the Father-in-Law of Caiaphas (<reference osisRef="John.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.18.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen27390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27391" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>:<div eID="gen27391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And they led Him away to Annas first; for he was father-in-law to Caiaphas, which was the high priest that same year--</hi>This successful Annas, as Ellicott remarks, was appointed high priest by Quirinus, A.D. 12, and after holding the office for several years, was deposed by Valerius Gratius, Pilate's predecessor in the procuratorship of Judea [Josephus, Antiquities, 18.2.1, &c.]. He appears, however, to have possessed vast influence, having obtained the high priesthood, not only for his son Eleazar, and his son-in-law Caiaphas, but subsequently for four other sons, under the last of whom James, the brother of our Lord, was put to death [Antiquities, 20.9.1]. It is thus highly probable that, besides having the title of "high priest" merely as one who had filled the office, he to a great degree retained the powers he had formerly exercised, and came to be regarded practically as a kind of rightful high priest.<div eID="gen27392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27393" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.14">Joh 18:14</reference>:<div eID="gen27393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27394" type="x-p"/> Now Caiaphas was he which gave counsel to the Jews, that it was expedient that one man should die for the people. See on <reference osisRef="John.11.51">Joh 11:51</reference>. What passed between Annas and our Lord during this interval the beloved disciple reserves till he has related the beginning of Peter's fall. To this, then, as recorded by our own Evangelist, let us meanwhile listen.<div eID="gen27394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27395" type="x-p"/> Peter Obtains Access within the Quadrangle of the High Priest's Residence, and Warms Himself at the Fire (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.53">Mr 14:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.54">54</reference>). <div eID="gen27395" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c25903ceabc0e0fc25206bfa88d5f50f6ae5b3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14170"/><div sID="gen27396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14170"/><hi type="bold">53. And they led Jesus away to the high priest: and with him were assembled--</hi>or rather, "there gathered together unto him."<div eID="gen27396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes--</hi>it was then a full and formal meeting of the Sanhedrim. Now, as the first three Evangelists place all Peter's denials of his Lord after this, we should naturally conclude that they took place while our Lord stood before the Sanhedrim. But besides that the natural impression is that the scene around the fire took place overnight, the second crowing of the cock, if we are to credit ancient writers, would occur about the beginning of the fourth watch, or between three and four in the morning. By that time, however, the Council had probably convened, being warned, perhaps, that they were to prepare for being called at any hour of the morning, should the Prisoner be successfully secured. If this be correct, it is fairly certain that only the last of Peter's three denials would take place while our Lord was under trial before the Sanhedrim. One thing more may require explanation. If our Lord had to be transferred from the residence of Annas to that of Caiaphas, one is apt to wonder that there is no mention of His being marched from the one to the other. But the building, in all likelihood, was one and the same; in which case He would merely have to be taken perhaps across the court, from one chamber to another. <div eID="gen27397" type="x-p"/>
entries.995d969b4e3ab3fe07d03d150b7a324b88e0fe17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14171"/><div sID="gen27398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14171"/><hi type="bold">54. And Peter followed him afar off, even into--</hi>or "from afar, even to the interior of."<div eID="gen27398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the palace of the high priest--</hi>"An oriental house," says Robinson, "is usually built around a quadrangular interior court; into which there is a passage (sometimes arched) through the front part of the house, closed next the street by a heavy folding gate, with a smaller wicket for single persons, kept by a porter. The interior court, often paved or flagged, and open to the sky, is the hall, which our translators have rendered 'palace,' where the attendants made a fire; and the passage beneath the front of the house, from the street to this court, is the porch. The place where Jesus stood before the high priest may have been an open room, or place of audience on the ground floor, in the rear or on one side of the court; such rooms, open in front, being customary. It was close upon the court, for Jesus heard all that was going on around the fire, and turned and looked upon Peter (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>)."<div eID="gen27399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he sat with the servants, and warmed himself at the fire--</hi>The graphic details, here omitted, are supplied in the other Gospels. <reference osisRef="John.18.18">Joh 18:18</reference>:<div eID="gen27400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And the servants and officers stood there--</hi>that is, in the hall, within the quadrangle, open to the sky.<div eID="gen27401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who had made a fire of coals--</hi>or charcoal (in a brazier probably).<div eID="gen27402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for it was cold--</hi>John alone of all the Evangelists mentions the material, and the coldness of the night, as Webster and Wilkinson remark. The elevated situation of Jerusalem, observes Tholuck, renders it so cold about Easter as to make a watch fire at night indispensable.<div eID="gen27403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And Peter stood with them and warmed himself--</hi>"He went in," says Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.58">Mt 26:58</reference>), "and sat with the servants to see the end." These two minute statements throw an interesting light on each other. His wishing to "see the end," or issue of these proceedings, was what led him into the palace, for he evidently feared the worst. But once in, the serpent coil is drawn closer; it is a cold night, and why should not he take advantage of the fire as well as others? Besides, in the talk of the crowd about the all-engrossing topic he may pick up something which he would like to hear. Poor Peter! But now, let us leave him warming himself at the fire, and listening to the hum of talk about this strange case by which the subordinate officials, passing to and fro and crowding around the fire in this open court, would while away the time; and, following what appears the order of the Evangelical Narrative, let us turn to Peter's Lord.<div eID="gen27404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus Is Interrogated by Annas--</hi>His Dignified Reply--Is Treated with Indignity by One of the Officials--His Meek Rebuke (<reference osisRef="John.18.19-John.18.23">Joh 18:19-23</reference>).<div eID="gen27405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27406" type="x-p"/> We have seen that it is only the Fourth Evangelist who tells us that our Lord was sent to Annas first, overnight, until the Sanhedrim could be got together at earliest dawn. We have now, in the same Gospel, the deeply instructive scene that passed during this non-official interview.<div eID="gen27406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27407" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.19">Joh 18:19</reference>:<div eID="gen27407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The high priest--</hi>Annas.<div eID="gen27408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then asked Jesus of His disciples and of His doctrine--</hi>probably to entrap Him into some statements which might be used against Him at the trial. From our Lord's answer it would seem that "His disciples" were understood to be some secret party.<div eID="gen27409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27410" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.20">Joh 18:20</reference>.<div eID="gen27410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world--</hi>compare <reference osisRef="John.7.4">Joh 7:4</reference>. He speaks of His public teaching as now a past thing--as now all over.<div eID="gen27411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27412" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ever taught in the synagogue and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort--</hi>courting publicity, though with sublime noiselessness.<div eID="gen27412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and in secret have I said nothing--</hi>rather, "spake I nothing"; that is, nothing different from what He taught in public: all His private communications with the Twelve being but explanations and developments of His public teaching. (Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Is 45:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">48:16</reference>).<div eID="gen27413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27414" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.21">Joh 18:21</reference>:<div eID="gen27414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27415" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Why askest thou Me? ask them which heard Me what I have said to them--</hi>rather, "what I said unto them."<div eID="gen27415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold, they know what I said--</hi>From this mode of replying, it is evident that our Lord saw the attempt to draw Him into self-crimination, and resented it by falling back upon the right of every accused party to have some charge laid against Him by competent witnesses.<div eID="gen27416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27417" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.22">Joh 18:22</reference>:<div eID="gen27417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And when He had thus spoken, one of the officers which stood by struck Jesus with the palm of his hand, saying, Answerest Thou the high priest so?--</hi>(see <reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Is 50:6</reference>). It would seem from <reference osisRef="Acts.23.2">Ac 23:2</reference> that this summary and undignified way of punishment what was deemed insolence in the accused had the sanction even of the high priests themselves.<div eID="gen27418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27419" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.23">Joh 18:23</reference>:<div eID="gen27419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus answered him, If I have spoken evil--</hi>rather, "If I spoke evil," in reply to the high priest.<div eID="gen27420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27421" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bear witness of the evil; but if well, why smitest thou Me?--</hi>He does not say "if not evil," as if His reply had been merely unobjectionable; but "if well," which seems to challenge something altogether fitting in the remonstrance. He had addressed to the high priest. From our Lord's procedure here, by the way, it is evident enough that His own precept in the Sermon on the Mount--that when smitten on the one cheek we are to turn to the smiter the other also (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">Mt 5:39</reference>)--is not to be taken to the letter.<div eID="gen27421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27422" type="x-p"/> Annas Sends Jesus to Caiaphas (<reference osisRef="John.18.24">Joh 18:24</reference>).<div eID="gen27422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27423" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="John.18.24">Joh 18:24</reference>.<div eID="gen27423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Now Annas had sent Him bound unto Caiaphas the high priest--</hi>On the meaning of this verse there is much diversity of opinion; and according as we understand it will be the conclusion we come to, whether there was but one hearing of our Lord before Annas and Caiaphas together, or whether, according to the view we have given above, there were two hearings--a preliminary and informal one before Annas, and a formal and official one before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrim. If our translators have given the right sense of the verse, there was but one hearing before Caiaphas; and then <reference osisRef="John.18.24">Joh 18:24</reference> <hi type="bold">is to be read as a parenthesis, merely supplementing what was said in <reference osisRef="John.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>. This is the view of Calvin, Beza, Grotius, Bengel, De Wette, Meyer, Lucke, Tholuck. But there are decided objections to this view. First: We cannot but think that the natural sense of the whole passage, embracing <reference osisRef="John.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.19-John.14.24">14, 19-24</reference>, is that of a preliminary non-official hearing before "Annas first," the particulars of which are accordingly recorded; and then of a transference of our Lord from Annas to Caiaphas. Second: On the other view, it is not easy to see why the Evangelist should not have inserted <reference osisRef="John.18.24">Joh 18:24</reference> immediately after <reference osisRef="John.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>; or rather, how he could well have done otherwise. As it stands, it is not only quite out of its proper place, but comes in most perplexingly. Whereas, if we take it as a simple statement of fact, that after Annas had finished his interview with Jesus, as recorded in <reference osisRef="John.18.19-John.18.23">Joh 18:19-23</reference>, he transferred Him to Caiaphas to be formally tried, all is clear and natural. Third: The pluperfect sense "had sent" is in the translation only; the sense of the original word being simply "sent." And though there are cases where the aorist here used has the sense of an English pluperfect, this sense is not to be put upon it unless it be obvious and indisputable. Here that is so far from being the case, that the pluperfect "had sent" is rather an unwarrantable interpretation than a simple translation of the word; informing the reader that, according to the view of our translators, our Lord "had been" sent to Caiaphas before the interview just recorded by the Evangelist; whereas, if we translate the verse literally--</hi>"Annas sent Him bound unto Caiaphas the high priest"--we get just the information we expect, that Annas, having merely "precognosced" the prisoner, hoping to draw something out of Him, "sent Him to Caiaphas" to be formally tried before the proper tribunal. This is the view of Chrysostom and Augustine among the Fathers; and of the moderns, of Olshausen, Schleiermacher, Neander, Ebrard, Wieseler, Lange, Luthardt. This brings us back to the text of our second Gospel, and in it to<div eID="gen27424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27425" type="x-p"/> The Judicial Trial and Condemnation of the Lord Jesus by the Sanhedrim (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.55-Mark.14.64">Mr 14:55-64</reference>).<div eID="gen27425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27426" type="x-p"/> But let the reader observe, that though this is introduced by the Evangelist before any of the denials of Peter are recorded, we have given reasons for concluding that probably the first two denials took place while our Lord was with Annas, and the last only during the trial before the Sanhedrim. <div eID="gen27426" type="x-p"/>
entries.c53f16b5e8cd645e1ba2971fd0ee3d71681e9f1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14172"/><div sID="gen27427" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14172"/><hi type="bold">55. And the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.59">Mt 26:59</reference>) says they "sought false witness." They knew they could find nothing valid; but having their Prisoner to bring before Pilate, they behooved to make a case.<div eID="gen27427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and found none--</hi>none that would suit their purpose, or make a decent ground of charge before Pilate. <div eID="gen27428" type="x-p"/>
entries.89490608231b5529b947bdb3fc72e4d6e7eaffa7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14173"/><div sID="gen27429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14173"/><hi type="bold">56. For many bare false witness against him--</hi>From their debasing themselves to "seek" them, we are led to infer that they were bribed to bear false witness; though there are never wanting sycophants enough, ready to sell themselves for naught, if they may but get a smile from those above them: see a similar scene in <reference osisRef="Acts.6.11-Acts.6.14">Ac 6:11-14</reference>. How is one reminded here of that complaint, "False witnesses did rise up: they laid to my charge things that I knew not" (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.11">Psa 31:11</reference>)!<div eID="gen27429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but their witness agreed not together--</hi>If even two of them had been agreed, it would have been greedily enough laid hold of, as all that the law insisted upon even in capital cases (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.6">De 17:6</reference>). But even in this they failed. One cannot but admire the providence which secured this result; since, on the one hand, it seems astonishing that those unscrupulous prosecutors and their ready tools should so bungle a business in which they felt their whole interests bound up; and, on the other hand, if they had succeeded in making even a plausible case, the effect on the progress of the Gospel might for a time have been injurious. But at the very time when His enemies were saying, "God hath forsaken Him; persecute and take Him; for there is none to deliver Him" (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.11">Psa 71:11</reference>), He whose Witness He was and whose work He was doing was keeping Him as the apple of His eye, and while He was making the wrath of man to praise Him, was restraining the remainder of that wrath (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Psa 76:10</reference>). <div eID="gen27430" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cc172e5eeb30784c30c180209ec45f44df7ea15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14174"/><div sID="gen27431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14174"/><hi type="bold">57. And there arose certain, and bare false witness against him--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.60">Mt 26:60</reference>) is more precise here: "At the last came two false witnesses." As no two had before agreed in anything, they felt it necessary to secure a duplicate testimony to something, but they were long of succeeding. And what was it, when at length it was brought forward?<div eID="gen27431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying--</hi>as follows: <div eID="gen27432" type="x-p"/>
entries.66c3e7cb31b89e4559ff44897a34afa20c62efaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14175"/><div sID="gen27433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14175"/><hi type="bold">58. We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and within three days I will build another made without hands--</hi>On this charge, observe, first, that eager as His enemies were to find criminal matter against our Lord, they had to go back to the outset of His ministry, His first visit to Jerusalem, more than three years before this. In all that He said and did after that, though ever increasing in boldness, they could find nothing. Next, that even then, they fix only on one speech, of two or three words, which they dared to adduce against Him. Further, they most manifestly pervert the speech of our Lord. We say not this because in Mark's form of it, it differs from the report of the words given by the Fourth Evangelist (<reference osisRef="John.2.18-John.2.22">Joh 2:18-22</reference>)--the only one of the Evangelists who reports it all, or mentions even any visit paid by our Lord to Jerusalem before His last--but because the one report bears truth, and the other falsehood, on its face. When our Lord said on that occasion, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up," they might, for a moment, have understood Him to refer to the temple out of whose courts He had swept the buyers and sellers. But after they had expressed their astonishment at His words, in that sense of them, and reasoned upon the time it had taken to rear the temple as it then stood, since no answer to this appears to have been given by our Lord, it is hardly conceivable that they should continue in the persuasion that this was really His meaning. But finally, even if the more ignorant among them had done so, it is next to certain that the ecclesiastics, who were the prosecutors in this case, did not believe that this was His meaning. For in less than three days after this they went to Pilate, saying, "Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was yet alive, after three days I will rise again" (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.63">Mt 27:63</reference>). Now what utterance of Christ known to His enemies, could this refer to, if not to this very saying about destroying and rearing up the temple? And if so, it puts it beyond a doubt that by this time, at least, they were perfectly aware that our Lord's words referred to His death by their hands and His resurrection by His own. But this is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Mark.14.59">Mr 14:59</reference>. <div eID="gen27433" type="x-p"/>
entries.80240785c3678d6cf4a536b80c6fc6b681b2f6ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14176"/><div sID="gen27434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14176"/><hi type="bold">59. But neither so did their witness agree together--</hi>that is, not even as to so brief a speech, consisting of but a few words, was there such a concurrence in their mode of reporting it as to make out a decent case. In such a charge everything depended on the very terms alleged to have been used. For every one must see that a very slight turn, either way, given to such words, would make them either something like indictable matter, or else a ridiculous ground for a criminal charge--would either give them a colorable pretext for the charge of impiety which they were bent on making out, or else make the whole saying appear, on the worst view that could be taken of it, as merely some mystical or empty boast. <div eID="gen27434" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e1f608e5d2e5e9a0877643f8062e32508f62f61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14177"/><div sID="gen27435" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14177"/><hi type="bold">60. Answerest thou nothing? what is it which these witness against thee?--</hi>Clearly, they felt that their case had failed, and by this artful question the high priest hoped to get from His own mouth what they had in vain tried to obtain from their false and contradictory witnesses. But in this, too, they failed. <div eID="gen27435" type="x-p"/>
entries.60cb886b6af06059e0e88b416524642824708adb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14178"/><div sID="gen27436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14178"/><hi type="bold">61. But he held his peace, and answered nothing--</hi>This must have nonplussed them. But they were not to be easily baulked of their object.<div eID="gen27436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Again the high priest--</hi>arose (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.62">Mt 26:62</reference>), matters having now come to a crisis.<div eID="gen27437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">asked him, and said unto him, Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?--</hi>Why our Lord should have answered this question, when He was silent as to the former, we might not have quite seen, but for Matthew, who says (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.63">Mt 26:63</reference>) that the high priest put Him upon solemn oath, saying, "I adjure Thee by the living God, that Thou tell us whether Thou be the Christ, the Son of God." Such an adjuration was understood to render an answer legally necessary (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Le 5:1</reference>). (Also see on <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>.) <div eID="gen27438" type="x-p"/>
entries.63f45741e7ceac12d6a790e8a2d359ff6b75cf16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14179"/><div sID="gen27439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14179"/><hi type="bold">62. And Jesus said, I am--</hi>or, as in Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">Mt 26:64</reference>), "Thou hast said [it]." In Luke, however (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.70">Lu 22:70</reference>), the answer, "Ye say that I am," should be rendered--as De Wette, Meyer, Ellicott, and the best critics agree that the preposition requires--"Ye say [it], for I am [so]." Some words, however, were spoken by our Lord before giving His answer to this solemn question. These are recorded by Luke alone (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.67">Lu 22:67</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.68">68</reference>): "Art Thou the Christ [they asked]? tell us. And He said unto them, If I tell you, ye will not believe: and if I also ask [interrogate] "you, ye will not answer Me, nor let Me go." This seems to have been uttered before giving His direct answer, as a calm remonstrance and dignified protest against the prejudgment of His case and the unfairness of their mode of procedure. But now let us hear the rest of the answer, in which the conscious majesty of Jesus breaks forth from behind the dark cloud which overhung Him as He stood before the Council. (Also see on <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>.)<div eID="gen27439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>in that character.<div eID="gen27440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven--</hi>In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">Mt 26:64</reference>) a slightly different but interesting turn is given to it by one word: "Thou hast said [it]: nevertheless"--We prefer this sense of the word to "besides," which some recent critics decide for--"I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sit on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven." The word rendered "hereafter" means, not "at some future time" (as to-day "hereafter" commonly does), but what the English word originally signified, "after here," "after now," or "from this time." Accordingly, in <reference osisRef="Luke.22.69">Lu 22:69</reference>, the words used mean "from now." So that though the reference we have given it to the day of His glorious Second Appearing is too obvious to admit of doubt, He would, by using the expression, "From this time," convey the important thought which He had before expressed, immediately after the traitor left the supper table to do his dark work, "Now is the Son of man glorified" (<reference osisRef="John.13.31">Joh 13:31</reference>). At this moment, and by this speech, did He "witness the good confession" emphatically and properly, as the apostle says in <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">1Ti 6:13</reference>. Our translators render the words there, "Who before Pontius Pilate witnessed"; referring it to the admission of His being a King, in the presence of Cæsar's own chief representative. But it should be rendered, as Luther renders it, and as the best interpreters now understand it, "Who under Pontius Pilate witnessed," &c. In this view of it, the apostle is referring not to what our Lord confessed before Pilate--which, though noble, was not of such primary importance--but to that sublime confession which, under Pilate's administration, He witnessed before the only competent tribunal on such occasions, the Supreme Ecclesiastical Council of God's chosen nation, that He was THE Messiah, and THE Son of the Blessed One; in the former word owning His Supreme Official, in the latter His Supreme Personal, Dignity. <div eID="gen27441" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c96c286a79d85c08afe2cebdbbde2fdc2d699f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14180"/><div sID="gen27442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14180"/><hi type="bold">63. Then the high priest rent his clothes--</hi>On this expression of horror of blasphemy, see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.37">2Ki 18:37</reference>.<div eID="gen27442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27443" type="x-p"/> and saith, What need we any further witnesses? (Also see on <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>.) <div eID="gen27443" type="x-p"/>
entries.36a36422a6507ce2bedbdd0d4f96021ace568943: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14181"/><div sID="gen27444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14181"/><hi type="bold">64. Ye have heard the blasphemy--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="John.10.33">Joh 10:33</reference>). In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.71">Lu 22:71</reference>), "For we ourselves have heard of His own mouth"--an affectation of religious horror. (Also see on <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>.)<div eID="gen27444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what think ye?--</hi>"Say what the verdict is to be."<div eID="gen27445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they all condemned him to be guilty of death--</hi>or of a capital crime, which blasphemy against God was according to the Jewish law (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.16">Le 24:16</reference>). Yet not absolutely all; for Joseph of Arimathea, "a good man and a just," was one of that Council, and "he was not a consenting party to the counsel and deed of them," for that is the strict sense of the words of <reference osisRef="Luke.23.50">Lu 23:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.23.51">51</reference>. Probably he absented himself, and Nicodemus also, from this meeting of the Council, the temper of which they would know too well to expect their voice to be listened to; and in that case, the words of our Evangelist are to be taken strictly, that, without one dissentient voice, "all [present] condemned him to be guilty of death."<div eID="gen27446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27447" type="x-p"/> The Blessed One Is Now Shamefully Entreated (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.65">Mr 14:65</reference>).<div eID="gen27447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27448" type="x-p"/> Every word here must be carefully observed, and the several accounts put together, that we may lose none of the awful indignities about to be described. <div eID="gen27448" type="x-p"/>
entries.412682f403fb7960e75580ae231ade3b65fe4fd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14182"/><div sID="gen27449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14182"/><hi type="bold">65. And some began to spit on him--</hi>or, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.26.67">Mt 26:67</reference>, "to spit in [into] His face." Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.63">Lu 22:63</reference>) says in addition, "And the men that held Jesus mocked him"--or cast their jeers at Him. (Also see on <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>.)<div eID="gen27449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to cover his face--</hi>or "to blindfold him" (as in <reference osisRef="Luke.22.64">Lu 22:64</reference>).<div eID="gen27450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to buffet him--</hi>Luke's word, which is rendered "smote Him" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.63">Lu 22:63</reference>), is a stronger one, conveying an idea for which we have an exact equivalent in English, but one too colloquial to be inserted here.<div eID="gen27451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">began to say unto him, Prophesy--</hi>In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.68">Mt 26:68</reference>) this is given more fully: "Prophesy unto us, thou Christ, Who is he that smote Thee?" The sarcastic fling at Him as "the Christ," and the demand of Him in this character to name the unseen perpetrator of the blows inflicted on Him, was in them as infamous as to Him it must have been, and was intended to be, stinging.<div eID="gen27452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the servants did strike him with the palms of their hands--</hi>or "struck Him on the face" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.64">Lu 22:64</reference>). Ah! Well did He say prophetically, in that Messianic prediction which we have often referred to, "I gave My back to the smiters, and My cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not My face from shame and spitting!" (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Is 50:6</reference>). "And many other things blasphemously spake they against Him" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.65">Lu 22:65</reference>). This general statement is important, as showing that virulent and varied as were the recorded affronts put upon Him, they are but a small specimen of what He endured on that dark occasion.<div eID="gen27453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27454" type="x-p"/> Peter's First Denial of His Lord (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.66-Mark.14.68">Mr 14:66-68</reference>). <div eID="gen27454" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8c99ad8122e82fb893f844e5b738df8291cc7d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14183"/><div sID="gen27455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14183"/><hi type="bold">66. And as Peter was beneath in the palace--</hi>This little word "beneath"--one of our Evangelist's graphic touches--is most important for the right understanding of what we may call the topography of the scene. We must take it in connection with Matthew's word (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.69">Mt 26:69</reference>): <hi type="bold">"Now Peter sat without in the palace"--</hi>or quadrangular court, in the center of which the fire would be burning; and crowding around and buzzing about it would be the menials and others who had been admitted within the court. At the upper end of this court, probably, would be the memorable chamber in which the trial was held--open to the court, likely, and not far from the fire (as we gather from <reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>), but on a higher level; for (as our verse says) the court, with Peter in it, was "beneath" it. The ascent to the Council chamber was perhaps by a short flight of steps. If the reader will bear this explanation in mind, he will find the intensely interesting details which follow more intelligible.<div eID="gen27455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there cometh one of the maids of the high priest--</hi>"the damsel that kept the door" (<reference osisRef="John.18.17">Joh 18:17</reference>). The Jews seem to have employed women as porters of their doors (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.13">Ac 12:13</reference>). <div eID="gen27456" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d83dae4f66302f9154d0c29f62deb945583df32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14184"/><div sID="gen27457" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14184"/><hi type="bold">67. And when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked upon him--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.56">Lu 22:56</reference>) is here more graphic; "But a certain maid beheld him as he sat by the fire"--literally, "by the light," which, shining full upon him, revealed him to the girl--"and earnestly looked upon him"--or, "fixed her gaze upon him." His demeanor and timidity, which must have attracted notice, as so generally happens, "leading," says Olshausen, "to the recognition of him."<div eID="gen27457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and said, And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth--</hi>"with Jesus the Nazarene," or, "with Jesus of Galilee" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.69">Mt 26:69</reference>). The sense of this is given in John's report of it (<reference osisRef="John.18.17">Joh 18:17</reference>), "Art not thou also one of this man's disciples?" that is, thou as well as "that other disciple," whom she knew to be one, but did not challenge, perceiving that he was a privileged person. In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.56">Lu 22:56</reference>) it is given as a remark made by the maid to one of the by-standers--"this man was also with Him." If so expressed in Peter's hearing--drawing upon him the eyes of every one that heard it (as we know it did, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.70">Mt 26:70</reference>), and compelling him to answer to it--that would explain the different forms of the report naturally enough. But in such a case this is of no real importance. <div eID="gen27458" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a8573e02bb3e1bbe8b164605dbc54331547101f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14185"/><div sID="gen27459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14185"/><hi type="bold">68. But he denied--</hi>"before all" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.70">Mt 26:70</reference>).<div eID="gen27459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, I know not, neither understand I what thou sayest--</hi>in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.57">Lu 22:57</reference>), "I know Him not."<div eID="gen27460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And he went out into the porch--</hi>the vestibule leading to the street--no doubt finding the fire-place too hot for him; possibly also with the hope of escaping--but that was not to be, and perhaps he dreaded that, too. Doubtless by this time his mind would be getting into a sea of commotion, and would fluctuate every moment in its resolves.<div eID="gen27461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">AND THE COCK CREW--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.22.34">Lu 22:34</reference>). This, then, was the First Denial.<div eID="gen27462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27463" type="x-p"/> Peter's Second Denial of His Lord (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.69">Mr 14:69</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.70">70</reference>).<div eID="gen27463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27464" type="x-p"/> There is here a verbal difference among the Evangelists, which without some information which has been withheld, cannot be quite extricated. <div eID="gen27464" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb66f337d3ca80cdaca1d3b88c14771d07848cb5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14186"/><div sID="gen27465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14186"/><hi type="bold">69. And a maid saw him again--</hi>or, "a girl." It might be rendered "the girl"; but this would not necessarily mean the same one as before, but might, and probably does, mean just the female who had charge of the door or gate near which Peter now was. Accordingly, in <reference osisRef="Matt.26.71">Mt 26:71</reference>, she is expressly called "another [maid]." But in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.58">Lu 22:58</reference>) it is a male servant: "And after a little while [from the time of the first denial] <hi type="bold">another"--</hi>that is, as the word signifies, "another male" servant. But there is no real difficulty, as the challenge, probably, after being made by one was reiterated by another. Accordingly, in John (<reference osisRef="John.18.25">Joh 18:25</reference>), it is, "They said therefore unto him, &c.--as if more than one challenged him at once.<div eID="gen27465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and began to say to them that stood by, This is one of them--</hi>or, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.26.71">Mt 26:71</reference>--"This [fellow] was also with Jesus the Nazarene." <div eID="gen27466" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0ffb4b358eaca4f47c5109aca64a45501162136: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14187"/><div sID="gen27467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14187"/><hi type="bold">70. And he denied it again--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.58">Lu 22:58</reference>), "Man, I am not." But worst of all in Matthew--"And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.72">Mt 26:72</reference>). This was the Second Denial, more vehement, alas! than the first.<div eID="gen27467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27468" type="x-p"/> Peter's Third Denial of His Lord (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.70-Mark.14.72">Mr 14:70-72</reference>). <div eID="gen27468" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14188"/><div sID="gen27469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14188"/><hi type="bold">70. And a little after--</hi>"about the space of one hour after" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.59">Lu 22:59</reference>).<div eID="gen27469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27470" type="x-p"/> they that stood by said again to Peter, Surely thou art one of them: <hi type="bold">for thou art a Galilean, and thy speech agreeth thereto--</hi>"bewrayeth [or 'discovereth'] thee" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.73">Mt 26:73</reference>). In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.59">Lu 22:59</reference>) it is, "Another confidently affirmed, saying, Of a truth this [fellow] also was with him: for he is a Galilean." The Galilean dialect had a more Syrian cast than that of Judea. If Peter had held his peace, this peculiarity had not been observed; but hoping, probably, to put them off the scent by joining in the fireside talk, he was thus discovered. The Fourth Gospel is particularly interesting here: "One of the servants of the high priest, being his kinsman [or kinsman to him] whose ear Peter cut off, saith, Did not I see thee in the garden with Him?" (<reference osisRef="John.18.26">Joh 18:26</reference>). No doubt his relationship to Malchus drew his attention to the man who had smitten him, and this enabled him to identify Peter. "Sad reprisals!" exclaims Bengel. Poor Peter! Thou art caught in thine own toils; but like a wild bull in a net, thou wilt toss and rage, filling up the measure of thy terrible declension by one more denial of thy Lord, and that the foulest of all. <div eID="gen27470" type="x-p"/>
entries.750c72ce3770a18bee52ca9839f52439575a6409: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14189"/><div sID="gen27471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14189"/><hi type="bold">71. But he began to curse--</hi>"anathematize," or wish himself accursed if what he was now to say was not true.<div eID="gen27471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and to swear--</hi>or to take a solemn oath.<div eID="gen27472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27473" type="x-p"/> saying, I know not this man of whom ye speak. <div eID="gen27473" type="x-p"/>
entries.90523820dec39edd13ce076c483606a6771f0362: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14190"/><div sID="gen27474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14190"/><hi type="bold">72. And the second time the cock crew--</hi>The other three Evangelists, who mention but one crowing of the cock--and that not the first, but the second and last one of Mark--all say the cock crew "immediately," but Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.60">Lu 22:60</reference>) says, "Immediately, while he yet spake, the cock crew." Alas!--But now comes the wonderful sequel.<div eID="gen27474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27475" type="x-p"/> The Redeemer's Look upon Peter, and Peter's Bitter Tears (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.72">Mr 14:72</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.62">62</reference>).<div eID="gen27475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27476" type="x-p"/> It has been observed that while the beloved disciple is the only one of the four Evangelists who does not record the repentance of Peter, he is the only one of the four who records the affecting and most beautiful scene of his complete restoration (<reference osisRef="John.21.15-John.21.17">Joh 21:15-17</reference>).<div eID="gen27476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27477" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>:<div eID="gen27477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And the Lord turned and looked upon Peter--</hi>How? it will be asked. We answer, From the chamber in which the trial was going on, in the direction of the court where Peter then stood--in the way already explained. See on <reference osisRef="Mark.14.66">Mr 14:66</reference>. Our Second Evangelist makes no mention of this look, but dwells on the warning of his Lord about the double crowing of the cock, which would announce his triple fall, as what rushed stingingly to his recollection and made him dissolve in tears.<div eID="gen27478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus said unto him, Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. And when he thought thereon, he wept--</hi>To the same effect is the statement of the First Evangelist (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.75">Mt 26:75</reference>), save that like "the beloved physician," he notices the "bitterness" of the weeping (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.62">Lu 22:62</reference>). The most precious link, however, in the whole chain of circumstances in this scene is beyond doubt that "look" of deepest, tenderest import reported by Luke alone (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.61">Lu 22:61</reference>). Who can tell what lightning flashes of wounded love and piercing reproach shot from that "look" through the eye of Peter into his heart!<div eID="gen27479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27480" type="x-p"/> And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how He had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny Me thrice.<div eID="gen27480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27481" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.62">Lu 22:62</reference>:<div eID="gen27481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And Peter went out and wept bitterly--</hi>How different from the sequel of Judas' act! Doubtless the hearts of the two men towards the Saviour were perfectly different from the first; and the treason of Judas was but the consummation of the wretched man's resistance of the blaze of light in the midst of which he had lived for three years, while Peter's denial was but a momentary obscuration of the heavenly light and love to his Master which ruled his life. But the immediate cause of the blessed revulsion which made Peter "weep bitterly" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.75">Mt 26:75</reference>) was, beyond all doubt, this heart-piercing "look" which his Lord gave him. And remembering the Saviour's own words at the table, "Simon, Simon, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat; but I prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.31">Lu 22:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">32</reference>), may we not say that this prayer fetched down all that there was in that look to pierce and break the heart of Peter, to keep it from despair, to work in it "repentance unto salvation not to be repented of," and at length, under other healing touches, to "restore his soul?" (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.16.7">Mr 16:7</reference>). <chapter eID="Mark.14"/>

entries.98f19b7a696b5bb0b38e3cc1616186438775954d: <div eID="gen39638" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39639" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39640" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39640" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39639" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39641" type="x-p"/> The Jews conspire against Christ, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.1">Mar 14:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.2">Mar 14:2</reference>. He is anointed in the house of Simon the Leper, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.3-Mar.14.9">Mar 14:3-9</reference>. Judas Iscariot sells him to the chief priests for thirty pieces of money, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.10">Mar 14:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.11">Mar 14:11</reference>. He orders his disciples to prepare the passover, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.12-Mar.14.16">Mar 14:12-16</reference>. Predicts his approaching death, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.17-Mar.14.21">Mar 14:17-21</reference>. Institutes the holy eucharist, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.22-Mar.14.26">Mar 14:22-26</reference>. Foretells the unfaithfulness of his disciples in general, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.27">Mar 14:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.28">Mar 14:28</reference>, and Peter's denial, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.29-Mar.14.31">Mar 14:29-31</reference>. His agony in the garden, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.32-Mar.14.36">Mar 14:32-36</reference>. The disciples overcome by sleep, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.37-Mar.14.42">Mar 14:37-42</reference>. Judas comes with a mob from the chief priests, and betrays him with a kiss; they seize him, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.43-Mar.14.49">Mar 14:43-49</reference>. The disciples flee, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.50">Mar 14:50</reference>. A young man following, and about to be apprehended, makes his escape, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.51">Mar 14:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.52">Mar 14:52</reference>. Jesus is brought before the chief priests, and Peter follows at a distance, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.53">Mar 14:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.54">Mar 14:54</reference>. He is examined, insulted, and abused, and condemned on false evidence, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.55-Mar.14.65">Mar 14:55-65</reference>. Peter thrice denies him, reflects on his wickedness, and repents of his sin, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.66-Mar.14.72">Mar 14:66-72</reference>. <div eID="gen39641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39642" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39643" type="x-p"/> Unleavened bread - After they began to eat unleavened bread: see on <reference osisRef="Mat.26.2">Mat 26:2</reference> (note).
entries.80b92b19e3f9751ea29c2c401af1b3816c959861: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39644" type="x-p"/> Alabaster box - Among critics and learned men there are various conjectures concerning the alabaster mentioned by the evangelists: some think it means a glass phial; others, that it signifies a small vessel without a handle, from α negative and λαβη, a handle; and others imagine that it merely signifies a perfume or essence bottle. There are several species of the soft calcareous stone called alabaster, which are enumerated and described in different chemical works. <div eID="gen39644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39645" type="x-p"/> Spikenard - Or nard. An Indian plant, whose root is very small and slender. It puts forth a long and small stalk, and has several ears or spikes even with the ground, which has given it the name of spikenard: the taste is bitter, acrid, and aromatic, and the smell agreeable. Calmet. <div eID="gen39645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39646" type="x-p"/> Very precious - Or rather, unadulterated: this I think is the proper meaning of πιστικης. Theophylact gives this interpretation of the passage: "Unadulterated hard, and prepared with fidelity." Some think that πιστικη is a contraction of the Latin spicatae, and that it signifies the spicated nard, or what we commonly call the spikenard. But Dr. Lightfoot gives a different interpretation. Πιστικη he supposes to come from the Syriac פיסתקא pistike, which signifies the acorn: he would therefore have it to signify an aromatic confection of nard, maste, or myrobalane. See his Hebrew and Talmudical Exercitations; and see Scheuchzer's Physica Sacra. <div eID="gen39646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39647" type="x-p"/> She brake the box - Rather, she broke the seal. This is the best translation I can give of the place; and I give it for these reasons: <div eID="gen39647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39648" type="x-p"/> 1. That it is not likely that a box exceedingly precious in itself should be broken to get out its contents. <div eID="gen39648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39649" type="x-p"/> 2. That the broken pieces would be very inconvenient if not injurious to the head of our Lord, and to the hands of the woman. <div eID="gen39649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39650" type="x-p"/> 3. That it would not be easy effectually to separate the oil from the broken pieces. And, <div eID="gen39650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39651" type="x-p"/> 4. That it was a custom in the eastern countries to seal the bottles with wax that held the perfumes; so that to come at their contents no more was necessary than to break the seal, which this woman appears to have done; and when the seal was thus broken, she had no more to do than to pour out the liquid ointment, which she could not have done had she broken the bottle. <div eID="gen39651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39652" type="x-p"/> The bottles which contain the gul i attyr, or attyr of roses, which come from the east, are sealed in this manner. See a number of proofs relative to this point in Harmer's Observations, vol. iv. 469. Pouring sweet-scented oil on the head is common in Bengal. At the close of the festival of the goddess Doorga, the Hindoos worship the unmarried daughters of Brahmins: and, among other ceremonies, pour sweet-scented oil on their heads. Ward's Customs.
entries.ea589896ec96f485e465707ce8d5f91bb464195f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen39652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39653" type="x-p"/> It might have been sold - το μυρον, This ointment, is added by ABCDKL, thirty-five others, Ethiopic, Armenian, Gothic, all the Itala except one. Griesbach has received it into the text. The sum mentioned here would amount to nearly 10 sterling.
entries.9434958bc459cfbc264b6d7143df1eb8a1cd5c53: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39654" type="x-p"/> To anoint my body to the burying - Εις τον ενταφιασμον, against, or in reference to, its embalmment, thus pointing out my death and the embalmment of my body, for the bodies of persons of distinction were wrapped up in aromatics to preserve them from putrefaction. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.26.12">Mat 26:12</reference> (note).
entries.b6b3ccbb4bc6f523a748a8337be091c868e409db: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39655" type="x-p"/> For a memorial of her - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.26.13">Mat 26:13</reference> (note).
entries.584d66ccd06860278afabc41520361337ecb4123: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen39655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39656" type="x-p"/> They were glad - The joy that arises from the opportunity of murdering an innocent person must be completely infernal.
entries.2043dbff95824c0b8a37ec754c83b620d60d7a6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39657" type="x-p"/> Bearing a pitcher of water - How correct is the foreknowledge of Jesus Christ! Even the minutest circumstances are comprehended by it! An honest employment, howsoever mean, is worthy the attention of God; and even a man bearing a pitcher of water is marked in all his steps, and is an object of the merciful regards of the Most High. This man was employed in carrying home the water which was to be used for baking the unleavened bread on the following day; for on that day it was not lawful to carry any: hence they were obliged to fetch it on the preceding evening.
entries.89197c1d13eff774f3fe8d0a56e1fbbba5a44e05: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen39657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39658" type="x-p"/> Say ye to the good man of the house - ειπατε τῳ οικοδεσποτῃ - Say ye to the master of the house. The good man and the good woman mean, among us, the master and mistress of the house. A Hindoo woman never calls her husband by his name; but simply, the man of the house. <div eID="gen39658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39659" type="x-p"/> Where is the guest chamber? - Respectable householders, says Mr. Ward, have a room which they call the strangers' room, (utit' hu-shala), which is especially set apart for the use of guests. This appears to have been the custom in Judea also.
entries.a514824ae8632da11d4512082a5c7dea5563ea49: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39660" type="x-p"/> Furnished - Spread with carpets - εστρωμενον - so this word is often used. See Wakefield. But it may also signify the couches on which the guests reclined when eating. It does not appear that the Jews ate the passover now, as their fathers did formerly, standing, with their shoes on, and their staves in their hands.
entries.5d76f976915af74beeafa7061a40d5d163652293: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39661" type="x-p"/> And another said, Is it I? - This clause is wanting in BCLP, seventeen others, Syriac, Persic, Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Vulgate, and four of the Itala. Griesbach leaves it doubtful: others leave it out.
entries.3aedd9314f68ae2b6643d557169aeedab976230a: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen39661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39662" type="x-p"/> That dippeth with me in the dish - In the east, persons never eat together from one dish, except when a strong attachment subsists between two or more persons of the same caste; in such a case one invites another to come and sit by him and eat from the same dish. This custom seems to have existed among the Jews; and the sacred historian mentions this notice of our Lord's, It is one of the twelve, that dippeth with me in the dish, to mark more strongly the perfidy of the character of Judas.
entries.90132dbbf830557acdb91f23dd66c85f560d7720: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39663" type="x-p"/> Goeth - That is, to die. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.26.24">Mat 26:24</reference> (note).
entries.3862653cc0aed1dd024880f0c3f126d4476c5f7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen39663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39664" type="x-p"/> Eat - This is omitted by many MSS. and versions, but I think without reason. It is found in the parallel places, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.26">Mat 26:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.24">1Cor 11:24</reference>. entries.06180440a3de963a9d37802af8b8b5a17395e274: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen39664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39665" type="x-p"/> That Thou - Συ is added by ABEGHKLMS - V, eighty-eight others, Syriac, Arabic, Persic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Slavonic, Vulgate, Saxon, Theophylact, and Euthymsus. entries.f2c9056f8e99edaac7084297588ff44971c4162c: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen39665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39666" type="x-p"/> Abba, Father - This Syriac word, which intimates filial affection and respect, and parental tenderness, seems to have been used by our blessed Lord merely considered as man, to show his complete submission to his Father's will, and the tender affection which he was conscious his Father had for him, Abba, Syriac, is here joined to ὁ πατηρ, Greek, both signifying father; so St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Rom 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal 4:6</reference>. The reason is, that from the time in which the Jews became conversant with the Greek language, by means of the Septuagint version and their commerce with the Roman and Greek provinces, they often intermingled Greek and Roman words with their own language. There is the fullest evidence of this fact in the earliest writings of the Jews; and they often add a word of the same meaning in Greek to their own term; such as מרי קירי, Mori, κυριε my Lord, Lord; פילי שער, pili, πυλη, shuar, gate, gate: and above, אבא, πατηρ, father, father: see several examples in Schoettgen. The words אבי and אבא appear to have been differently used among the Hebrews; the first Abbi, was a term of civil respect; the second, Abba, a term of filial affection. Hence, Abba, Abbi, as in the Syriac version in this place, may be considered as expressing, My Lord, my Father. And in this sense St. Paul is to be understood in the places referred to above. See Lightfoot.
entries.6d56f951f6d0505fb00968d1ff4831f9aa70b228: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen39666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39667" type="x-p"/> Saith unto Peter - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.26.40">Mat 26:40</reference> (note).
entries.167efe99ad97ea1b277301713c48d25473f2ae7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 51</hi> <div eID="gen39667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39668" type="x-p"/> A certain young man - Probably raised from his sleep by the noise which the rabble made who came to apprehend Jesus, having wrapped the sheet or some of the bed-clothing about him, became thereby the more conspicuous: on his appearing, he was seized; but as they had no way of holding him, but only by the cloth which was wrapped round him, he disengaged himself from that, and so escaped out of their hands. This circumstance is not related by any other of the evangelists.
entries.7131b2095b0dd254048916a33c51566b4b1c9988: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen39668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39669" type="x-p"/> And he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked - It has often been intimated, by the inhabitants of India, that a European in strait clothes must be in great danger when his clothes take fire. From their loose clothing they can suddenly disengage themselves. When two Hindoos are engaged in a violent quarrel, and one seizes the clothing of the other, often the latter will leave his clothes in the hands of his opponent, and flee away naked. This seems to have been the case with the person mentioned above. See Ward's Customs.
entries.4a8f7b080aea2973531b294e34b52838192c6d0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 54</hi> <div eID="gen39669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39670" type="x-p"/> Peter followed - On Peter's denial, see <reference osisRef="Mat.26.57">Mat 26:57</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen39670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39671" type="x-p"/> At the fire - Προς το φως, literally, at the light, i.e. a fire that cast considerable light, in consequence of which, the maid servant was the better able to distinguish him: see <reference osisRef="Mar.14.67">Mar 14:67</reference>.
entries.3bf2ed04fa12a6107692052d3ceb75f4a57b3ecf: <hi type="bold">Verse 61</hi> <div eID="gen39671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39672" type="x-p"/> Of the Blessed? - Θεου του ευλογητου, Or, of God the blessed one. Θεου, is added here by AK, ten others, Vulgate, and one of the Itala. It might be introduced into the text, put in Italics, if the authority of the MSS. and versions be not deemed sufficient. It appears necessary for the better understanding of the text. The adjective, however, conveys a good sense by itself, and is according to a frequent Hebrew form of speech.
entries.cc58e396e39701c9f2636fb4207f11c2e2c60164: <hi type="bold">Verse 72</hi> <div eID="gen39672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39673" type="x-p"/> And when he thought thereon, he wept - Or, he fell a weeping. This Mr. Wakefield thinks comes nearest to the original, επιβαλων εκλαιε. Others think it means the wrapping of his head in the skirts of his garment, through shame and anguish. Others think that επιβαλων rather refers to the violence, or hurry, with which he left the place, being impelled thereto by the terrors and remorse of his guilty conscience. Our own translation is as good as any.  <chapter eID="Mark.14"/> <div eID="gen39673" type="x-p"/>

entries.61b634ce833fc020eb9c0846df43f88e1a4f60db:
Verse 3. Ointment. This word does not convey quite the proper meaning. This was a perfume: it was used only to give a pleasant odour, and was liquid.

Of spikenard. The nard, from which this perfume was made, is a plant of the East Indies, with a small slender stalk, and a heavy, thick root. The best perfume is obtained from the root, though the stalk and fruit are used for that purpose.

And she brake the box. This may mean no more than that she broke the seal of the box. so that it could be poured out. Boxes of perfumes are often sealed, or made fast with wax, to prevent the perfume from escaping. It was not likely that she would break the box itself when it was unnecessary; and when the unguent, being liquid, would have been wasted, when it was very precious. Nor from a broken box or phial, could she easily have poured it on his head.

Verse 41. It is enough. There has been much difficulty in determining the meaning of this phrase. Campbell translates it, "All is over;" i.e., the time when you could have been of service to me is gone by. They might have aided him by watching for him, when they were sleeping; but now the time was past, and he was already, as it were, in the hands of his enemies. It is not improbable, however, that after his agony some time elapsed before Judas came. He had required them to watch, i. e., to keep awake, during that season of agony. After that, they might have been suffered to sleep, while Jesus watched alone. As he saw Judas approach, he probably roused them, saying, It is sufficient--as much repose has been taken as is allowable--the enemy is near, and the Son of man is about to be betrayed.

entries.c4983dba275d3943a6827f654359172b08a40cca:
Verse 51. A certain young man. Who this was, we have no means of determining. That he was not one of the apostles is dear. It is probable that he was of one of the neighbouring villages or houses, and was roused from sleep by the noise made by the rabble, and came to see what was doing; nor is it known why this circumstance is recorded by Mark. It is omitted by all the other evangelists. It may have been recorded to show that the conspirators had instructions to take the apostles as well as Jesus; and supposing him to be one of them, they laid hold of him to take him before the high priest.

A linen cloth cast about his naked body. He was roused from sleep, and probably threw around him what was most convenient. They slept in linen bedclothes commonly, and he seized a part of the clothes, and hastily threw it round him.

The young men. The Roman soldiers, They were called young men because they were made up chiefly of youth originally. This was a Jewish mode of speaking. See Gen 14:24, 2Sam 2:14, Isa 13:18.

Laid hold on him. Supposing him to be one of the apostles.

entries.4cec4a6a39e116dde07f88066c68e991d0496ad2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.14.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.14.24" sID="gen102470" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.24">Mark 14:24</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">This is my blood. </hi>I have already remarked that, when we are told that <hi type="italic">the blood is to be shed </hi>—<hi type="italic"> </hi>according to the narrative of Matthew — <hi type="italic">for the remission of sins,</hi> these words direct us to the sacrifice of the death of Christ, without the remembrance of which the Lord’s Supper is never observed in a proper manner. And, indeed, it is impossible for believing souls to be satisfied in any other way than by being assured that God is pacified towards them.<div eID="gen102471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102472" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Which is shed for many. </hi>By the word <hi type="italic">many </hi>he means not a part of the world only, but the whole human race; for he contrasts many with one; as if he had said, that he will not be the Redeemer of one man only, but will die in order to deliver <hi type="italic">many </hi>from the condemnation of the curse. It must at the same time be observed, however, that by the words <hi type="italic">for you, </hi>as related by Luke — Christ directly addresses the disciples, and exhorts every believer to apply to his own advantage <hi type="italic">the shedding of blood </hi>Therefore, when we approach to the holy table, let us not only remember in general that the world has been redeemed by the blood of Christ, but let every one consider for himself that his own sins have been expiated. <note n="197"> <div sID="gen102473" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que la purgation de ses pechez a esté faite</foreign>;” — “that satisfaction has been made for his own sins.”<div eID="gen102473" type="x-p"/> </note> <div eID="gen102472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102474" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Of the new testament. </hi>Luke and Paul (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.25">1 Corinthians 11:25</reference>) express it differently, <hi type="italic">the new testament in my blood, </hi>but the meaning is the same; for it is only by a spiritual drinking of <hi type="italic">blood </hi>that this <hi type="italic">covenant </hi>is ratified, so as to be firm and stable. Yet it may easily be inferred from it, how foolishly superstitious the <hi type="italic">Papists</hi> and others of the same stamp are in rigidly adhering to the words; for, with all their bluster, they cannot set aside this exposition of the Holy Spirit, that <hi type="italic">the cup </hi>is called <hi type="italic">blood, </hi>because <hi type="italic">it is the new testament in blood</hi>. But the same argument applies to the <hi type="italic">bread; </hi>from which it will follow that it is called <hi type="italic">the body; </hi>because it is <hi type="italic">the testament in</hi> <hi type="italic">the body</hi> They have no right now to contend that we ought to rely on the simple words of Christ, and shut our ears against expositions from without. It is Christ himself that speaks, and surely they will not deny that he is well qualified to interpret his own words. Now Christ openly declares that he called the <hi type="italic">bread his body</hi>, for no other reason than because he has made with us an everlasting covenant, that, the sacrifice having been once offered, we may now be spiritually fed.<div eID="gen102474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102475" type="x-p"/>There are two things here which deserve our attention; for from the word <hi type="italic">testament, </hi>or <hi type="italic">covenant, </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="el">διαθήκη</foreign>,) we infer that a promise is included in the Holy Supper. This refutes the error of those who maintain that faith is not aided, nourished, supported, or increased by the sacraments; for there is always a mutual relation between the <hi type="italic">covenant </hi>of God and the faith of men. By the epithet <hi type="italic">New </hi>he intended to show that the ancient figures now cease, and give way to a firm and everlasting covenant. There is an indirect contrast, therefore, between this mystery and the shadows of the law; from which it is evident how much better our condition is than that of our fathers, since, in consequence of the sacrifice which was completed on the cross, we possess the truth in perfection.<div eID="gen102475" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.14.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102470" osisID="Mark.14.24" type="section"/>

Mark 14:26. When they had sung a hymn. Our three Evangelists leave out those divine discourses,
“Ces beaux propos pleins de majest, divine;” — “those beautiful discourses, full of divine majesty.”
which John relates to have been delivered by our Lord, both in the house and on the road. For, as we have elsewhere stated, their object was rather to embrace the history of our Lord’s actions than his doctrine. They glance only at the fact, that he went out of his own accord where Judas was to come; and their object is to inform us that he made such an arrangement of his time, as willingly to meet him who betrayed him.

entries.fbdab6ddd5896be05ee852b5f4cca2670da12c74:
Mark 14:51. And a young man. How some persons have come to dream that this was John
“Aucuns ont songé que c’estoit Jean, l’un des Apostres;” — “some have dreamed that it was John, one of the Apostles.”
I know not, nor is it of much importance to inquire. The chief point is, to ascertain for what purpose Mark has related this transaction. I think that his object was, to inform us that those wicked men — as usually happens in riotous assemblies stormed and raved without shame or modesty; which appeared from their seizing a young man who was unknown to them, and not suspected of any crime, so that he had difficulty in escaping out of their hands naked. For it is probable that the young man, who is mentioned, had some attachment to Christ, and, on hearing the tumult by night, without stopping to put on his clothes, and covered only with a linen garment, came either to discover their traps, or, at least, that he might not be wanting in a duty of friendship.
“Ou, pour le moins à fin de faire devoir d’ami envers Jesus Christ;” — “or, at least, in order to perform the duty of a friend towards Jesus Christ.”
We certainly perceive — as I just now said — that those wicked men raged with cruel violence, when they did not even spare a poor young man, who had left his bed, almost naked, and run, on hearing the noise.

               <ns0:p n="46">46 And they laid their hands on him, and took him.</ns0:p>
